video_title: Luke Burgis on Mimetic Desire, Catholicism, and the Age of Social Contagion
transcript: TYLER COWEN: Hello, everyone, and welcome back  to Conversations with Tyler. Today I am sitting   here personally with Luke Burgis, one of my  favorite current thinkers. He’s author of the   bestselling book Wanting, and his recent  work is just coming out. It is called The   One and the Ninety-Nine: Forging Identity in  the Age of Social Contagion. Luke, welcome. LUKE BURGIS: Thanks for having  me, Tyler. Good to be here. COWEN: I should add you are  also director and founder   of the Cluny Institute. What is your title? BURGIS: I’m assistant professor of practice  in the business school at Catholic University. COWEN: Great. I have questions  about your latest book and your   thought more generally. Is the current  age of pessimism and despair ending? BURGIS: I think it might get worse  before it gets better. I hope it ends.   There’s been a lot of talk among friends of mine  who are very pro-tech accelerationists that the   pope is going to really come down on tech in  his new papal encyclical, which at the time of   our conversation is not out yet. There’s been  a lot of speculation about it. I think they’re   absolutely wrong, for instance, in that case.  I think he’s going to be very optimistic about   what AI can do for humanity, of course, with  some cautions about the way that it develops. I think that even among my tech friends,  I’m seeing a lot of pessimism for   what a thinker like the pope might say  and not even giving him the benefit of   the doubt that we might be entering an age  where we can actually learn more about what   it means to be human than less. That might  lead to a renaissance in the humanities,   for instance. I think AI is performing a  kind of via negativa on the human person,   maybe even the human soul, in helping us  discover who we are. To me, that’s very exciting. COWEN: I agree with you about the pope, but  if social contagion is such a dominant force,   how does the age of pessimism get turned around?  What’s the mechanism by which things will flip? BURGIS: We need some more optimists, and then we  can hope for a good contagion with the optimists. COWEN: Why doesn’t the negative  contagion just get stronger and   stronger and overwhelm everything, and  we all drown in a sea of terribleness? BURGIS: The negative contagion and pessimism  can’t go on forever. I think that there are   cultural and societal release valves for  that kind of thing. Vibe shifts happen.   There’s the scapegoat mechanism. I don’t know  if we’ll talk about Girard today. I think that   there are things that correct. Sometimes  we over-correct. I just don’t see the   age of pessimism lasting. I think sometimes if  something happens that is traumatic and tragic,   like a serious war, even worse than the wars  that we currently see in the world today,   maybe it will take something like that to  actually help people build something. It   sounds a little bit paradoxical, but I think  sometimes optimism can arise out of tragedy. COWEN: Why does it seem in the data, at least,  that the Anglo world is especially so unhappy? BURGIS: The Anglo world, I think, especially  in the US, I really believe that we have some   bad ideas, what Byung-Chul Han has called  the achievement subject. It’s this very   Calvinist idea that I think has affected even  the way that we think about entrepreneurship,   which I’m extremely pro-entrepreneurship, but I  think that it’s in his book, The Burnout Society,   which was one of my favorite books. I  think he diagnoses the problem very well. We’ve internalized this idea that we always  have to be doing something. There is always   more to achieve. We’ve forgotten some of  the fundamental things that actually make   for a good life. Family structures, people  are not having children. You and I have   talked about the fertility crisis before. I  think that that achievement subject mentality   has affected the West through everything  from media to our business culture. I think we’re going to need to reevaluate that  as a society. I just got back from three and a   half weeks in Italy and I came back—I was going  to say I came back refreshed, but I traveled with   the toddler, so I can’t say that—I came back  wondering. For all of the economic stagnation   and problems that Italy has, do they also  have something right? People there actually   seem more joyful and optimistic, even than most  Americans that I know that are doing pretty well. COWEN: As a critique of modernity, is  Dostoevsky or Thomas Mann more on the mark? BURGIS: I’m very sympathetic to Thomas  Mann because I went to a seminary on   top of a hill in Italy for three years that  almost felt like a sanatorium in some ways.   I’m going to go with Dostoevsky, though,  because I think his book Demons diagnoses   what can happen at a psychic and spiritual level  when social contagion runs rampant. Of course,   having just written a book about social contagion,  I don’t think he’s mentioned in the book,   but Dostoevsky and some of the demonic elements,  whether you believe in demons or not, we can speak   of the demonic as something that seems to be  characterized by social contagion usually. COWEN: Here’s a question from GPT, and I quote,   “Name the kind of person who reads  your book, takes the thesis sincerely,   applies it carefully, and yet ends up  worse off.” What’s the story there? BURGIS: The new book or Wanting or both? COWEN: The new book. Both,  but they’re of a piece, right? BURGIS: They’re connected. Wanting is about  mimetic desire, and this book is a continuation   of that and how it plays out in social  dynamics, the self versus the crowd. I actually   think there’s a risk with my books and with any  nonfiction book or the exposure to any big idea,   especially one that purports to explain some  fundamental first principle about social life,   of thinking about it too much, making it a theory  of everything, over-psychologizing everything,   and losing sight of the concrete  realities and circumstances that we’re in. To give you an example, it’s been  said that once a novelist reads the   work of René Girard and understands  mimetic theory and mimetic desire,   it will ruin them as a novelist because now they  don’t think that they have any original ideas,   everything’s just mimetic. The way out of that  problem actually is to stop thinking about it   so dang much and to not impose that frame on  everything and to get back to the concrete   and the particulars of life, which is a kind of  antidote. I’m not saying don’t reflect and don’t   think and that we shouldn’t think about these  things, but there is such a thing as overthinking. COWEN: It’s a little bit like efficient  markets theory. Even if it’s true,   it’s better not to believe it? BURGIS: Yes. COWEN: Better for the world  and maybe better for you too.   Speaking of AI, will it make social contagion  stronger or weaker or in which ways? BURGIS: I would bet that it’s going  to make social contagion weaker. COWEN: Why? BURGIS: Because we’re leaving the age of  information and entering what I would call the age   of intelligence. AI, to give one example, I think,  will lead to highly customized, personalized   education and learning experiences. People  being able to construct and follow. If you’re   an autodidact, I think it will be very good for  you because you’ll be able to follow ideas to the   end. We used to have to just read the footnotes  and try to track down obscure books. I think   AI will make that process a lot easier and more  exciting. That is not a mimetic process. It’s not   a social contagion process. That is using the AI  to follow your own intellectual interests. I could   probably think of other ways that it will make  us less contagious, but that’s just one of them. COWEN: That might be part of what  flips us out of the pessimism? BURGIS: I think so. COWEN: Is that new emancipation? BURGIS: I’m incredibly excited by that. I’m  thinking about my own writing and my own work.   I’ve got all kinds of blind spots and limitations.  When I write something or when I’m thinking about   something, asking the AI, what are all the  implications of what I’ve said here to a bunch   of domains of life that I don’t really know that  much about, I’m always amazed by what it says. COWEN: What’s the story behind you  declining to work for Anthropic? BURGIS: Well, it wasn’t to work for  them, just to set the record straight. COWEN: Not to work for pay,  but to confer with them, right? BURGIS: Just to confer with  them, yes. There’s a lot that I   don’t want to say, but I can tell you  more than I think I’ve said so far. COWEN: Sure. BURGIS: I always probe people’s motivations. In  this case, I had a back and forth with some folks   at Anthropic. I was asking basic questions like,  what’s next after this? They basically invited 14,   15 people out for a couple of days  to comment on Claude’s constitution.   I think they were all Christians, and  they were interested in virtue ethics and   what Christianity might have to add to  the development of making Claude be good. I asked basic questions like, “What do you mean  by be? Philosophically, like that. What does that   mean? What does it mean for Claude to be good? It  seems like your discovery of virtue ethics, and   they were using the word discernment, is you’ve  landed on something that Ignatius and the Jesuits   had figured out 500 years ago. What’s next? Is  it just the two days, and what comes after that?”   The more that I talked to them—people do this all  the time; it’s why people like to meet the pope,   for instance—I didn’t know how genuine it was. I  thought that they were looking for a way to say,   “We did this thing, we conferred with  some Christians, we’re the good guys,   we’re building the good AI.” Then the way that it  was pitched to me was very much like, if I care   about the future and the good of humanity, then  this is definitely something that I could do. It was framed like a moral imperative, not only  by people at Anthropic, but even by people that   know me, by fellow Christians. I said, “I  do think I have some moral responsibilities,   and there’s some moral imperatives in my  life, but flying out to San Francisco to   consult for Anthropic for free is not one  of them.” I don’t think that makes me a bad   person. It was just in the communication  with them, I felt like something was off. COWEN: Just philosophically, putting  aside your theological views,   but what do you think of effective altruism  as a normative philosophy? That has guided,   at least, some parts of AI production, right? BURGIS: Yes. It seems to have  guided many parts of it. I think   ultimately it hasn’t proved very successful in  doing some of the things that it set out to do.   I guess when we go back to the  beginning of effective altruism,   I’m unclear on how effectiveness is defined  by each person that practices it in different   ways. I don’t think that there’s enough  conversation on what the goals really are,   and it’s—and this will not surprise you—ultimately  very materialistic and doesn’t account for things   like the quality of relationships, depth,  culture. The things that can be measured,   usually with effective altruism, are often not the  things that I think are most important in life. COWEN: If I ask you a question like,   why do men and women seem to be so far apart  these days, politically and aesthetically,   you think you would have a better answer  to that than the effective altruists would. BURGIS: What’s their answer to that question? COWEN: I’m not sure, but what’s your answer? BURGIS: I’m not sure if that’s true. COWEN: It’s political polarization. If you  poll them on politics, men are more right-wing. BURGIS: Oh, we’re talking  specifically about politics. COWEN: Women are more left-wing, but as you  know, measured sex seems to be going down;   certainly, childbearing,  which we measure pretty well,   is going down. Marriage is a more complicated  story, but for some socioeconomic groups,   it’s down. There’s just much less dating.  Everyone claims the dating apps are broken.   There was a piece in New Statesman about, in  Britain, angry young women are very upset at   the men that they encounter. It just seems to be  worse than usual, the gap between men and women? BURGIS: Yes. I think technology is largely  to blame for that, the way that it sorts   things that it thinks men should see versus  things that women should see. It increases   the political polarization for everybody,  but in particular, between the genders,   I think that it plays a huge role. I think that  the way that men and women even meet each other,   the way that dating works, is very, very  different than the way that it used to be. We often sort based on what we think our  preferences are before we’ve had a chance   to encounter a flesh and human person of the  opposite sex, and perceptions are formed,   often wrongly. The woman that I eventually  married, I never would have found her if I   was using a dating app, for instance.  I think technology has exacerbated   some of the false perceptions that we have  about the opposite sex and what people believe. That’s especially true when it comes to  men and women because the algorithms,   the way that the social contagion  works, it knows that we are different.   We are men and women, and it exacerbates all of  the differences and doesn’t do much to promote   common understanding. I believe that men and women  are complementary, different but complementary,   and that’s not necessarily  a very popular view anymore. COWEN: At what point does being  anti-mimetic itself become a mimetic   identity, and do you see some signs  of that in Silicon Valley? Everyone’s   supposed to be contrarian. There’s a  kind of false contrarianism. You don’t   even know anymore what’s a contrarian point of  view. Are we at that stage with Girardianism? BURGIS: I think Girard would be  relatively mortified that mimetic   theory was very mimetic and so popular.  I think he himself worried about that,   and that was a running joke while he was still  alive in his circle at Stanford. I do think it’s   an issue. It goes back to why I said we shouldn’t  think about it too much. The book is titled The   One and the Ninety-Nine. The message, as  you know from having read it, is not that   everybody should become a rugged individualist  and that the goal is to become the one. I think that’s incredibly dangerous. It’s  actually, in a world where all of the focus   is on the one, maybe we need to think more  actually about the 99 and the relationship   between the one and the 99 and the way that  the group and the self affect one another. I   think the focus has actually swung way too far  in the direction of the one. I mean, all of us   are the one in some sense, but the challenge of  today is how do we live in communities without   clustering in communities where everybody shares  the same values and thinks the same things?   Those are the most boring communities for me.  I don’t want to be in one of those communities,   but I get invited to them almost on  a daily basis, and I usually decline. COWEN: Let’s say we put you in charge, either  of the government or of certain voluntary norms,   and you can change one thing. What’s the thing you   would change within the realm  of it being somewhat feasible? BURGIS: In charge as a political leader or a CEO? COWEN: You can either be dictator, or  you can be pope, or you can just be   the most influential person on moral  norms, and you can change one thing. BURGIS: If I were the dictator of the United  States—my fiscally conservative friends   will hate this one—I think we lack mediating  intermediary institutions between individuals   in the state and that communities, places  are healthier to the extent that they have   these odd places in between, whether third  places or just intermediary institutions. I would probably find a good musician in every  city who had some entrepreneurial spirit and was   interested in bringing people together—let’s  call it cities with over 100,000 people—and I   would give them startup funds to open jazz clubs  in every single city, and I would fund them from   my government. I would do probably a public  campaign to encourage—actually, I don’t know;   maybe the public campaign would backfire on  me because nobody likes being told what to do. COWEN: Become too mimetic. BURGIS: Forget that part. I think jazz  clubs in every city would go a long way   toward helping men and women. It would  probably actually go a long way toward   something nothing like jazz and alcohol to  help men and women learn to like each other. COWEN: Changing a voluntary  social norm, what would you pick?   Like young men lose interest in pornography? BURGIS: That one I’d definitely want to change. COWEN: What’s at the top of your list?  It gives us a sense of your priorities. BURGIS: It is. You named one that is at the top  of my list. I think it’s absolutely destroying   young men and women. The data is very clear  that women are watching a lot of porn, too. I   think that there are certain things that should be  made taboo. Porn is taboo in the sense that nobody   talks about it. I actually bring it up often  in my class because the data are something like   90 percent of the men in my class are watching  porn, and not quite that number with the women. I’ll often bring it up in class, and then  I’m shocked at how many students over the   course of a few years actually come talk to me  about it. I’m actually relatively in favor of   introducing friction into the process and how  easy that stuff can be found. It’s being found   by accident. There was a story in the Free Press  last year. I think it was a 13-year-old girl found   it by accident. She said the discovery of it  has become like a rite of passage for people,   and it’s not even one that they’re seeking.  It just happens to them. I think there has   to be some friction introduced in  that process, and I would do that. COWEN: In Girardian terms, is there  going to be a scapegoat that leads   to catharsis for us, or things remain unresolved? BURGIS: My understanding of Girard is that that  world is gone, the world in which we can have a   scapegoat that will lead to catharsis.  We’re past that. We’ve seen too much.   One of his fundamental points is that  Christianity has created the conditions   for the runaway violence precisely  because the scapegoats don’t work anymore. COWEN: Are we still in a  Christian society, ideologically? BURGIS: Yes, absolutely. I think even people  that would consider themselves very secular   have obviously adopted a lot of Christian  ideas, in the West, I assume you mean. COWEN: Sure, but say Japan. Is  Japan going to have a scapegoat? BURGIS: It would be more likely for Japan to have  a scapegoat than for any country in the West. I   think we’re very much in a Christian society,  and there are some people on the integralist   right that don’t realize how Christian  of a society we actually do live in. COWEN: You must know Rod Dreher. What do  you think of The Benedict Option? Withdraw. BURGIS: I want to do Rod justice, and I  think it’s easy to strawman Rod and say   that he’s just recommending that everybody  move to a small farm. I don’t think that’s   what he’s saying. I think what he  gets right is that every person,   every family—my wife and I are thinking through  this right now—is going to have to probably,   in the world of social contagion, if it’s as bad  as some people think that it is, and I think that   there are many things that are bad, will have  to take certain actions to protect themselves. If I don’t want my children watching porn  at a very young age, there’s certain things   that I’m going to have to do, and it will  involve putting boundaries between them   and the broader culture. I don’t think  it can be very prescriptive. I think   everybody’s case is very unique. I don’t plan  to move to Montana, but other people might. COWEN: They have the internet in Montana. I  would worry all the more in Montana, right? BURGIS: They have great internet in Montana.  I think that we live in a relatively Manichean   society. There’s a desire for purity. I  think the desire for purity is relatively   dangerous. It’s my disposition, I  think it’s my wife’s disposition,   to roll up my sleeves and just deal with  the messy world. I’ve noticed that every   time in my life where I’ve tried to flee it in  some way, I’ve actually ended up less happy. COWEN: I’m not saying you’ll ever do it, but what  does your escape fantasy look like? One of mine is   I’ll go live in a third-tier city in Mexico. I’m  not going to do it, but sometimes I think about   it. Cost of living would be very low. The food  would be amazing. I could improve my Spanish. BURGIS: It is moving to Genoa with my family,  making my US income, living in Italy. I love   Italy. I love the food. I love the people. I love  the culture. I feel lighter while I’m there. I   laugh more. We eat dinner later. I love everything  about it. It would probably be living in Italy for   the most part, or at least making that my home  base, brushing up on my Italian, working less. COWEN: Why Genoa? It’s a wonderful city.  It’s still medieval, right, in a funny way? BURGIS: It’s medieval. I think it’s  the most underrated city in Italy. COWEN: In Italy, I mean, yes. I agree. Yes. BURGIS: I think it’s the most  underrated city. You agree. COWEN: I took my wife there. She was stunned. “How  come no one goes to Genoa?” She was telling me. BURGIS: It’s close to Cinque Terre. It’s this city  that’s elevated. It has a fascinating history.   It was still a very functional port city. It  was really the most important city in Italy,   arguably the world, during when Spain was  a great power. It’s very cosmopolitan.   It reminds me of Marseille a little bit. It’s  vertical, breathtaking views. The people there,   they’re not very touristy. The Italians  there seem indifferent to you as a tourist. It just feels very, very homey. It’s so  close to a lot of other great things in   Italy. You can get to Torino relatively  easily. That whole area up there, Bra,   where the Slow Food movement originated, you’re  just in striking distance from everything. Nobody   I know that goes to Italy goes to Genoa. I plead  with them. I’m like, “Please, just go to Genoa.” COWEN: I am the exception. My wife sometimes talks  of wanting to live in the smaller towns nearby,   which we’re not going to do because we’re  slated for a third-tier city in Mexico,   but we’re not going to do that either. I sometimes  think of Northern Italy as a place where there   were fewer different dimensions for mimetic  desire. That is, more people dress the same.   There are fewer status dimensions, maybe less  room for eccentrics compared to America. Do   you think that’s true, or do you think I’m off  base? Paris is a bit like this also. There’s a   certain notion of what kind of shoes an  Italian man should wear. They wear them,   and they’re amazing, and actually more affordable  than here. There’s a sameness to some things. BURGIS: I don’t think the sameness is a bad  thing. I think the sameness is very charming.   The sprezzatura of an Italian man, the way that  an Italian man dresses, something I’ve never   been able to pull off in my life. For those  that don’t know what that sprezzatura means,   it means you put tremendous care into putting on  an outfit that looks like you didn’t think about   it at all, and somehow it comes together and looks  amazing. Even that seems highly mimetic to me,   the idea of sprezzatura. I love Naples. Naples  is maybe my second-favorite city in Italy. COWEN: It’s my second favorite, too. Maybe  it’s my favorite. That and Genoa, to me,   are the two undiscovered, less discovered gems. BURGIS: It makes sense why  we get along. Nobody goes to   Naples either. It’s too dirty. It’s  endless. I’ve heard all the excuses. COWEN: It’s become somewhat more  popular, though. There’ve been some   New York Times articles. The food  has drawn some people, I think. BURGIS: My test for whether or not I’ll get along  with somebody is their reactions to Naples after   they’ve been there. That’s my number one  test. To the Northern Italian question,   there’s a great book on Italy, if you haven’t  read it. It’s called The Italians by Luigi   Barzini in the ’60s. It’s just a fantastic book.  I think that the North has a little bit less of   the animated Italian gestures and spectacle  that you get in the South. It’s a little more   reserved. I would say that because of that,  it’s less mimetic than the South. I think that   disposition, that flamboyant way of being, is the  more mimetic thing about the South, about Naples. COWEN: Speaking of Barzini, what do  you think of his hypothesis that the   face an Italian will show you,  in terms of level of cheeriness,   depends on how your status is perceived?  He thinks they’re somewhat of a sad people,   but they seem happy to outsiders because they  put on that face for the higher-status outsiders. BURGIS: I wouldn’t disagree with Barzini  on Italian culture, so I’m not going to   disagree with him on that. He knows Italians much  better than I do. I think that the face in Italy,   maybe it’s like the smile in Thai. There’s  1,000 different smiles, and they all mean   something different. Italians are incredibly  good at reading the face and facial expressions,   but I think they have a different standard for  foreigners like me than they do for each other. COWEN: How is Italian Catholicism different? BURGIS: Depends on what part of Italy you’re in. COWEN: Say, Genoa, whatever part you know best. BURGIS: I think that, having spent a few weeks  there very recently and went to mass quite a   few times—I was there during Holy Week—it is  aesthetically very different. You typically   will walk into a very old church that has no  heating or AC, has absolutely terrible acoustics,   and you’ll find people wandering in and  out, like you would in an orthodox church.   It’s like walking around. I would say that it’s  relatively low liturgy compared to what you see. A lot of the revival in Catholicism here in  the US are high-liturgy things. I actually   found it to be somewhat difficult. I couldn’t  even hear the priests most of the time because   the sound system is really bad. I think that  the liturgy is really the test for me about   everything else that’s going on, and that’s the  sacramental life. The first thing I notice about   any Catholic church is how many times they  offer confession. I look at it right away,   and I can tell you 10 other things about that same  church and predict it with a very high degree. COWEN: What does that tell  you? Let’s say they offer   confession frequently. What do you then infer? BURGIS: I infer that it’s thriving. One could say  they offer confession frequently because they just   have a lot of people there that believe in the  sacrament of confession. I think it’s quite the   opposite. It turns out from every priest that  I’ve talked to that if you offer confession   frequently, maybe a few times a week or  daily, the lines just start to form. It’s   actually quite the opposite. You’ll have a lot  of priests that just start offering it more. The extremes are confessions available by  appointment only on Saturdays versus confession   before every mass. That is the number one signal  for me, and then how often they have adoration.   This is Catholic inside baseball here. It is like  politics. If I know your position on gun control,   I can, with a high degree of accuracy, predict  your position on 10 other clustered things. COWEN: Why is it that, at least in formal terms,  Italy has become so nonreligious? I get that   underneath the cultural structure, it may be quite  Catholic still, but the number of people who go   to church or who profess, say, a belief in the  Trinity seems fairly low. How did that happen? BURGIS: It seems like they’re almost tired of  their Catholicism. They’ve had it for so long.   It almost seems like cultural Judaism  to me. It’s maybe like the familiarity   breeds contempt. I don’t know, but that’s the  sense that I get. Like some politics in Italy,   I think Mussolini had something to do with it,  the Christian Democrats. I think that it was   such a part of their identity for so long, it  wasn’t handed down by the last few generations,   and there’s just a sense in  which it has become cultural. I met many Italians on this last trip  that would make the sign of the cross   if they heard an ambulance drive by or they  walked by an image of Madonna on a street   corner or something like that, but they  probably haven’t been to mass in years.   This has become very cultural. I don’t  know why, but I think that they’re tired. COWEN: What was it like  living next to Vatican City? BURGIS: Speaking of this, I was mortified when  one day I had to walk directly by St. Peter’s   very often just to get home up on the Janiculum  Hill. I walked by St. Peter’s one day and I didn’t   look at it, I didn’t think about it, and then I  was mortified and I realized it was too late to   go back because I had to be somewhere. Rome can  be a very difficult place to live as a person of   faith. When I got there, somebody said, Rome  will either strengthen your faith or lose it   as a Catholic because you will see  the dark underbelly of everything. You will see a lot of worldliness and you will  either come out of it with a more supernatural   vision of what the church is or you will come  out of it with your tail between your legs,   really worried about things. For me, it was really  not one of those two extremes. It was like I came   out of it not that much different than when I  went in. It was probably the three most formative   years of my life when I lived next to the Vatican  because it was an incredibly strange situation. I was a 31-year-old man who had owned  my own house in Las Vegas and suddenly   lived in what was essentially a dormitory with  250 other men, most of them younger than me.   The typical age for a seminarian is 20,  25 probably, with a shared bathroom on   every floor. Talk about a relatively mimetic  environment where we share so much in common.   I would also say because of that, it was one of  the funniest places that I’ve ever been because   one of the ways that you learn to live in  a situation like that is through comedy. COWEN: Why didn’t you become a priest? BURGIS: John Henry Newman said that  one should never tell the story of   their conversion or their vocational  discernment between tea and dessert.   It’s just too complex of a question. The easy  answer that I’ll give you, it’s not a cop-out,   is that I carefully discerned for a number  of years that it was not what I felt like I   was being called to do. I’ll tell you one of the  little parts of that story that helped me realize   that. I was studying theology at a pontifical  university in Rome, right in Piazza Navona. I was on my way to a fundamental theology  class in my second year in Rome. I was having   nagging doubts. Something felt a little bit  off in my discernment process. It turned out   that there was a Matthew Luhn who was a Pixar  animator. He played an instrumental role in   the development of the first Toy Story. He  was a storyboard guy. He worked with all of   these guys at Pixar. He happened to be in Rome  giving a master class on storytelling that day.   This is a very typical Italian story. The venue  you’re supposed to give the workshop at in Rome   did not allow him in due to some kind of  bureaucratic maintenance of the building. COWEN: Very Italian already. BURGIS: It’s incredibly Italian. He had to find an  emergency place to hold his workshop, and he held   it at my pontifical university. I don’t know the  backstory there, but he was there. I saw a sign,   “Matthew Luhn, Pixar, storytelling master class.”  It was not cheap. All these Italians paid to go.   I talked my way in, and I skipped class, and I  went to the storytelling class that day. I was so   lit up by that class that I realized that there  was something in me that craved this creative,   artistic, aesthetic thing. I think it ruined  theology for me for the rest of the year. COWEN: Aesthetics trumped theology? BURGIS: Von Balthasar wrote a whole aesthetic  treatise, the theological aesthetics. Theology   and aesthetics go hand in hand, really. He  understood the whole story of the incarnation,   like the acts of a play. I think that I’m  very much a von Balthasar Catholic in the   sense that I do see a lot of the goodness and  beauty and aesthetic characteristics of the   church as related to truth. It’s one of the ways  that we can come to the truth is through beauty. COWEN: Aesthetically, what is  it in Christianity that’s most   important to you personally? If  it were me—I’m not Christian—but   I might say Bach’s B minor mass or maybe  Monteverdi’s Vespers. What would you say? BURGIS:   Aesthetically, it is the liturgy. It is  a beautifully celebrated Catholic mass.   I’m not one of these pre-Vatican II guys  where I think that the Latin mass is the   only real mass. I do think that is incredibly  beautiful, though. I go to it every once in a   while because I think it’s very beautiful. I  actually came back to my faith through that   practice. It’s not one particular thing or piece  of artwork for me; it is the beauty of the ritual. We’ve lost ritual in the world today in many  cases. Seeing that, seeing the reverence,   seeing a church full of people shoulder  to shoulder on their knees in itself is   beautiful to me. I remember just seeing  everybody drop to their knees for the   first time when I went back to mass after not  having gone in a very long time. I remember   being struck by that’s not something I  would see anywhere else in the world. COWEN: If I speak to people who are Ethiopian  Christians or maybe Egyptian Coptic Christians,   possibly Armenian Christians, they will  communicate a sense that somehow they’re   in tune with an earlier, more fundamental  Christianity than what we have in many other   places. Does that argument carry any weight  with you? Are you tempted by that or no? BURGIS: A little bit. I don’t think that  it’s true, but I’m very attracted to   orthodoxy, to the liturgy. It is incredibly  beautiful. Even the divider that they have,   where the priest consecrates  the Eucharist behind a wall,   there’s a sense of mystery and transcendence to  that I really like. I think the world could use   more sense of mystery and more otherness. I  think one of the things that worries me a lot   about the church today is that the church  has become highly mimetic with the world. You have priests and influencers, they’re  on TikTok performing skits and things like   that. I think it’s incredibly unhelpful because  there needs to be a level of otherworldliness,   alterity, that I think the Eastern  Orthodox liturgy preserves in a way   even better than the new  Mass, the Novus Ordo does. COWEN: Do we need Protestantism in America  to keep print culture front and center?   Isn’t Catholic culture in some ways too  visual or too theatrical, and the Protestant   impulse is very good for broader society  because print is a more thoughtful medium? BURGIS: I love my Protestant brothers and sisters,  so I don’t want them to go away. I might want them   all to become Catholic, but I think that many,  many great things have come out of this tension.   I think generally good things do come out of  tension, and yes, the church is oral to more   of an extent than Protestantism is. I think it’s  interesting now because we’re entering a world   in which—I’m a big fan of Marshall McLuhan—but  it seems to me like the traditional forms of   written word, even traditional essays, that  is changing incredibly fast in the world that   we’re entering. AI is just going to change the  form of that, so I don’t know where that goes. COWEN: Now, you and Ross Douthat, you  both self-identify as Catholics. He’s   been on this podcast several times.  We’ve talked about religious issues.   If you had to pin down exactly where your  religious vision of Catholicism differs   from his in as fundamental a manner as  possible, how would you describe that? BURGIS: He might take more of a rationalist  approach than I do. And I believe in faith   and reason, as John Paul II said, are like two  wings by which one rises to the contemplation of   the truth. It goes back, for me, I mentioned,  aesthetics and beauty, so it’s the witness of   the saints that initially attracted to me.  It was the beauty, it was the tradition,   the continuity of the church and the world through  such a long time. Reading the lives of the saints   as a witness, for me, that has always been the  first step, not trying to think my way to it. I think Augustine had this beautiful phrase of  faith seeking understanding. What I’m not saying   is that we should not see—because the church has  a wonderful intellectual tradition—but I’m less of   an apologetics guy, maybe. I think the best chance  that I have to help somebody see what I see in   the church is not to try to convince them of the  argument of why Christianity is true, which is the   only good reason to be Christian, in my opinion.  It’s to take them to Rome, and bring them inside   a beautiful church to witness a beautiful mass, to  drink a lot of good wine, and have conversations   late into the night about the good, the true, and  the beautiful. That, to me, is the more circuitous   route. Maybe it’s not the fastest route, but I  would say it’s more of an aesthetic approach. COWEN: If the world today is enchanted,  or we should think of it as enchanted,   what are the most literal manifestations of  that? Of course, it would be the world itself,   but specific things. Are there  miracles happening commonly,   or how do you think about specific  events within that framework? BURGIS: I wouldn’t be surprised if there’s a  Marian apparition in my lifetime, like a big one.   I don’t know if it’ll be Our Lady of  Guadalupe, but I think that sometimes,   the enchantment requires that people need  to be open to enchantment to see it. There   are enchanting things going on all around us. The  world is not necessarily becoming more enchanted.   It’s us that are perceiving and noticing the  things to be enchanted by. That’s why I say maybe   I just have a sense that maybe there will be some  openness to things that seem supernatural. I don’t   know nearly enough about this. Speaking of Ross, I  know that he’s fascinated by the question of UFOs— COWEN: Sure. UAPs, yes. BURGIS: —but it seems as if even  this discourse that we’re in right   now points to a desire for some  extraterrestrial, supernatural,   enchanted things. We’re really trying to  find them, and we’re having a hard time. COWEN: J. D. Vance said he thought they  were demons. I don’t agree with that,   but I don’t find it crazy. BURGIS: I don’t find it crazy either,  as one who believes in demons. That’s   a better explanation than others that I’ve heard. COWEN: Do you think he, and  maybe you, have a Manichean   approach to Christianity, if demons are relevant? BURGIS: Well, demons are fundamental to  Christianity. The gospels are full of   stories of Jesus driving out demons. The Gerasene  demoniac is the most famous example of that.   He says, “We are legion,” and this is  the quintessential gospel story where   the demonic has and always has an element of  contagion because the entire herd is infected   by this demon and is driven off into the sea.  There’s nothing Manichean about that to me,   living in a world where demons are real,  where evil is real, and exorcisms are real. I’ve known my fair share of exorcists, and  they seem to be on the rise, by the way,   from what the data shows. Most of it’s  anecdotal. I don’t know how rigorously   they’re actually tracked. I think they are by the  church, but that is not public data. Anecdotally,   it seems like they’re on the rise.  Manichean is kind of there’s good,   and then there’s evil, and we have to  purify. Just admitting a world that   might have the demonic element in it,  there’s nothing Manichean about that. COWEN: If you think of Shiite Islam, which  sometimes is compared a bit to Catholicism,   relative to Sunni Islam at least, do you feel  any affinity to that approach? Obviously,   it’s missing the Trinity and Jesus and many other   fundamental things from your point  of view, but is there any kinship? BURGIS: I don’t know enough about Shiite Islam.   What would be one thing that might  be similar to Catholicism about it? COWEN: The world being enchanted, things and  truths being hidden, and the multiplication of   intermediaries as a way to get to those  truths seem to me much more Catholic,   if I had to say, and Sunni Islam seems much more  Protestant with an emphasis on the Quran itself. BURGIS: Well, given what you’ve just shared,  I probably would be if I learned more about   it. Seems to share some elements. The idea  that there are truths that are hidden is   something I would like to just drill down on  just for a second, because in Catholicism,   it’s that the truth has basically been revealed  fully in the person of Jesus Christ. The   alternative to that is Gnosticism, which is  generally the idea that there’s always some   hidden truth. It’s like Scientology. There’s  always this one more thing. If you just learn   this next thing, then that’s the pathway  to salvation is more and more knowledge. Very interestingly, when I read the  parable of the lost sheep in the gospels,   where Jesus tells the story of a shepherd  that has 100 sheep. One of them goes missing,   is lost. He leaves the 99 to go find it and  brings it back. There is a Gnostic gospel of   Thomas version of that same parable. In the  Gnostic gospel of Thomas, the sheep is not a   sinner that Jesus finds. The one lost sheep was  the smartest sheep. When Jesus finds the one,   he does not bring him back to the flock. He pats  him on the head and praises him for not being like   all of the other sheep, for being smart enough to  forge his own way, and to leave the herd and the   crowd, and all of the other dumb sheep. Now, that  is the Gnostic interpretation, just to be clear. I   find it very, very interesting and very indicative  of the times that we live in today, where I think   people would be more attracted to the Gnostic  interpretation than the traditional one. COWEN: The revelation of Jesus, again, within a  Christian framework, it’s not fully transparent.   There’s four Gospels. They have some differences,  if only of emphasis. There was a period where   there’s an Avignon papacy. You can count on  the church to interpret, but there’s a claim   that there’s two popes, who’s the real pope,  which is the real church. One way or another,   people had to make up their minds. Isn’t  there room again for hiddenness in that   framework, even if you adhere to a Catholic  perspective as fully as you might try to? BURGIS: Yes. One of the exciting things about  the faith, and being Catholic, is the adventure   of navigating a spiritual life and a religious  life that ultimately is your own. One part of   the tradition that I always find interesting  is personal divine revelation to individuals.   This goes to the heart of the question, the  hidden. Sister Faustina is a very famous Polish   saint. She was a nun. She died in her 20s, lived  in a convent, barely left her whole life. Then,   when she died, there were just diaries and  diaries filled with personal conversations   that she claimed to have with Jesus. This is  where the divine mercy, the famous painting.   She said that Jesus actually showed her how he  would like to be depicted in the painting to   show the world his divine mercy. That’s an example  of this personal revelation, which the church has   probed and decided that it’s worthy of sharing  and belief. The hiddenness is certainly there. COWEN: On the political right these days,  why do you think there’s now so much   mimetic antisemitism? It seems to have come from  nowhere. Maybe that’s an incorrect impression,   but haven’t you been shocked by how  much there is, and how open it’s become? BURGIS: I’ve been totally shocked by it. COWEN: What happened? BURGIS: Scandalized by it. I don’t know. I  hate to think that it’s always been there.   There’s two ways I think that one could  explain it. It’s either always been there,   and something has happened that makes  people show their true colors. I hope   that version of the story is not true. The  other version of the story, which I think   imputes less culpability to people, is that there  is some crazy mimetic thing happening right now.   It’s cool to be edgy or something like that and to  say things. You’ve got Nick Fuentes. I think he’s   incredibly influential, especially to a younger  generation, and that it is a mimetic thing that,   hopefully, people will snap out of once  it’s been exposed for what it really is. COWEN: The Luke Burgis production function.  What did you learn in your Wall Street years? BURGIS: How much I hate working on Wall  Street. I learned that efficient markets   theory is BS. All of the things that I learned  in a very good undergraduate business school   did not actually seem to be used in the  day-to-day. Maybe it was because I was a   lowly analyst at an investment bank. If I  had worked at a hedge fund, I would have   been enthralled by seeking alpha. Unfortunately,  I didn’t get to do that as an analyst who just put   together pitch decks and built financial models  in Excel. I learned that I wanted to take risks,   and I couldn’t wait to take those risks, so I did  not spend very long on Wall Street. It was less   than two years that I actually worked on Wall  Street. I left when I started my first company. COWEN: What did you learn starting  those businesses in Italy? BURGIS: Well, I never started a business in Italy. COWEN: You ran them from Italy? BURGIS: No, no, I was in Italy as a seminarian. COWEN: Okay. BURGIS: I ended up walking away from a company  in my late 20s to take up some time off,   and that eventually led me to enter the seminary  as I was on the pathway to becoming a priest. I   did organize my life so that I was on a board  while I was there. I didn’t let go completely,   but I let go of all of the operational stuff.  It was still a little distracting for me as I   was trying to study philosophy and theology,  and then would get reports about something   super technical going on a few thousand miles  away back home. I slowed down a lot in Italy.   Being an entrepreneur is incredibly difficult  because nobody ever tells you to stop,   and there’s always something else to do. It  helped me bring some balance back into my life. COWEN: Is there a book that the current  Luke would recommend to the 23-year-old   Luke that he would have hated but you  still think he should have been reading? BURGIS: Byung-Chul Han, The Burnout Society, I  would have hated that book as a 23-year-old. I   remember having an older investment banker come  speak to me when I was a senior and tell me   that I was gung-ho. I was saying, “If I can come  work at Goldman Sachs, I’ll work 80-hour weeks,   I’ll sleep in the office.” He really walked me  back from all of that language. He was like,   “Young man, that’s really not what  you want to do. That’s not really   the best approach here.” I thought he  was really lame. I thought, “This guy,   he’s not going to make it.” He wasn’t that  old. He’d been doing it for a few years. I   thought that he was just not ambitious enough. The  Burnout Society would have been a struggle for me. COWEN: What part of Silicon Valley,   if any, do you secretly admire more than  perhaps your audience expects from you? BURGIS: I really admire people getting  together to build things, usually,   without sorting by things like political  preference. The thing that I love about   Silicon Valley is solving real problems in the  world with the best people you can find working   in small teams together—wish the church did more  of this, should do more building, maybe, and less   talking about the ethics of AI—to actually  try to build things, experiment with things. I think the church probably needs a  workshop in Rome to actually start   building things. You can speak much more  intelligently about it. I admire so many   things about Silicon Valley. I miss the  energy of it. DC is very different energy.   It has created a culture. There are some  parts of it that I think can be dangerous,   but San Francisco is still the most important city  in the world, particularly because of the AI boom,   because it’s never been replicated anywhere  else. I think there’s a reason for that. COWEN: Why do you remain personally  so tied to the state of Michigan? BURGIS: Well, I spend my summers in Michigan,  most of my summers. I think it’s the greatest   state in the country. It has a lake that looks  like an ocean when you’re standing on it. There’s   something about the Midwest that I’ll never be  able to take it out of me, even having lived   in big cities. My dad was a truck driver.  My mom was a grade school art teacher and   artist. There’s kind of an earthiness, and it was  great growing up there. I hated it at the time,   but now I think about how wonderful it was to  have to go through the four seasons every year. COWEN: Where did you grow up, exactly in Michigan? BURGIS: Grand Rapids, Michigan, on the west  side of the state. Scraping the ice off of   the windshield at seven o’clock in the morning on  my way to school. All of those things, I think,   they do form some character. I love it. I  love the grittiness. I love Detroit. I’m a   little partial to the West side of Michigan  just because that’s where I’m from. I’ve   suffered as a Detroit Lions fan my entire  life. I think that the Upper Peninsula is   one of the hidden gems in the entire world.  I don’t know if you’ve ever been to the UP. COWEN: Of course, it’s wonderful. BURGIS: It’s just wonderful. COWEN: Highly underrated— BURGIS: It’s highly underrated. COWEN: —like Genoa. BURGIS: Yes. I try not to talk about  Michigan too much because Northern   Michigan, like the Traverse City area, is  getting written up in the New York Times,   which I hate to see anytime I see it, because it  is wonderful. Prices are totally out of control,   so I should probably just stop talking about  all the wonderful things about Michigan. COWEN: Now, your own Cluny Institute, do  you think of it as closer to a monastery,   a salon, a talent network, a way of  organizing a Christian counter elite,   all of those? How’s the way you would  present what it is or what it does? BURGIS: I would think of it as trying  to build a talent network and forming a   kind of artist colony and workshop for people  that have a religious sense or sensibility,   that are open to the transcendent, that  are smart, that care about serious ideas,   and that want to build real things in the world,  that really care about the vector of innovation.   It’s not just building, but it’s like a step  back, what should we be building? Trying to   find as many of those people as possible in the  world. It’s got a couple of different functions. One of them is it’s trying to operate as a bat  signal, putting things out into the world that   bring the right people out of the woodwork. That’s  certainly happening. Then there’s a part of it   where I want to work with people that are able to  work at the intersection of what I call Athens,   Jerusalem, and Silicon Valley. We don’t have to  silo those things. I think that Silicon Valley,   for instance, would be healthier if it actually  wasn’t as allergic to religious thinking,   for instance. I think religious thinking  could do Silicon Valley a lot of good. I’m   betting that if we can begin to find that  network, and invest in that talent network,   that 10 or 20 years from now, it will be  building some of the most important things in   the world. I don’t just mean companies. I mean  cultural things, aesthetic things, workshops,   things that will produce new forms of community,  maybe even a model for a new institution. The reason that I am so struck by the story of  the original Cluny is that it was an entirely   new kind of institution in its day. Even legally  speaking, right? Its original charter, the guy   that gave all of the money renounced his right to  have anything to do with the way that it operated.   It formed a network of over 1,200 Cluniac  monasteries. My imagination is struck by,   “Well, what does that look like today if  we can have networked workshops of people   that are all drawing inspiration, and talking  about ideas that are open to the religious sense?” COWEN: The original Cluny was also a pioneer  of accounting techniques. Is that correct? BURGIS: I know that a Franciscan invented  double-entry accounting. I know that,   but he wasn’t associated with Cluny.  There were all kinds of innovations,   architectural innovations, agricultural,  winemaking innovations that happened. It   was really the largest church in the world for 300  years, the most important institution in Europe,   in my opinion. It was the center of innovation  in Europe, out of the liturgical renewal that   it instituted, and it welcomed people in.  Monasteries, the Benedictine tradition,   has always been known for hospitality. No matter  who you were, if you’re sick, if you’re poor,   if you’re traveling, if you’re a pilgrim, you  could knock on the door, and you would be let in,   and you could stay for a day or two or longer,  and then you would be sent on your way. Cluny actually popularized the Camino de Santiago.  They’re the first ones that would send people on   the Camino de Santiago. I could go on and on about  all the things that Cluny did, but the people that   came into contact with it—it was worldly in  the sense that it interacted with politicians,   with builders, with the Romanesque, the masons in  Italy. It was incredibly worldly in that it opened   its door to all of those people and interacted  with them, and then somehow shaped them. Is   there a lay version of that? I’m obviously not  trying to build a monastery. I’m not a monk,   but I’m inspired by the way that it existed in the  world as a sign of something completely different. COWEN: Before the last two questions,  just another plug for your book. The title   is The One and the Ninety-Nine: Forging  Identity in the Age of Social Contagion.   Last two questions. First, I’m sure  you’ve been following the case of   Ben Sasse as of late. How do you think  you will deal with your pending death? BURGIS: I hope I can deal with it  as good as he has dealt with his.   It’s interesting because there’s Bryan Johnson  in the live forever campaign. He’s speaking at   a conference that I’m hosting this summer, and  directly following him as a Benedictine monk who,   part of the Benedictine tradition, is literally  meditating on your death every single day.   There’s the memento mori. The tradition of  keeping a skull on your desk, which I do.   I learned that when I was in seminary. It’s not a  macabre-looking skull. It’s actually from Mexico.   It’s incredibly painted with all these bright  colors. It is on my desk. It’s about this big,   but meditating on it and actually going  through it are two different things. I suppose that my hope is I draw a lot of  inspiration from Ben Sasse, that in C. S.   Lewis’s words, “One should die before they die  and die a series of small deaths to our ego.”   I’ve certainly had to do that several times  in my life. I’m sure they won’t be the last,   and I think that’s really the key. I can’t tell  you how much I admire him going and talking to   people. I can’t remember anybody that has died in  public since John Paul II, who really died a slow   death in public over many years. Unfortunately,  Ben Sasse, it’ll probably be much faster. There’s   a Catholic tradition of actually praying  for a good death. It’s to St. Joseph. COWEN: Final question: What will you do next? BURGIS: I plan to be building  Cluny for a very long time.   I’ve had an itch for a long time to do  something more artistic. I’ve had a novel   that I’ve thought about writing for a long time,  but it’s not easy to write serious nonfiction,   and then flip into a different mode. I don’t  know if that will take some kind of detox   period from the world of ideas. Maybe  I’ll need to go live in Italy for a year. I’m really inspired by creating new environments  and experimenting with new forms. I don’t think   it’s unrelated to the artistic project, but I  feel a really strong desire to do that. I hope   that Cluny is a place where I can do that out  of so I often think of, I am one artist in the   colony that is Cluny, and maybe whatever art  that I create, whether it’s a novel, a book,   or whether it’s a gallery, or some kind of  experience, or something like that. It will   just be a manifestation of what I hope Cluny will  help other people do. I want to open a restaurant,   but I probably won’t do that for another 30  years, until I can afford to lose a lot of money. COWEN: That’s in the US or in Italy? BURGIS: Probably in Italy. COWEN: Luke Burgis, thank you very much. BURGIS: Thanks for having me, Tyler.

transcript_segments.text: TYLER COWEN: Hello, everyone, and welcome back  to Conversations with Tyler. Today I am sitting
here personally with Luke Burgis, one of my  favorite current thinkers. He’s author of the
bestselling book Wanting, and his recent  work is just coming out. It is called The
One and the Ninety-Nine: Forging Identity in  the Age of Social Contagion. Luke, welcome.
LUKE BURGIS: Thanks for having  me, Tyler. Good to be here.
COWEN: I should add you are  also director and founder
of the Cluny Institute. What is your title?
BURGIS: I’m assistant professor of practice  in the business school at Catholic University.
COWEN: Great. I have questions  about your latest book and your
thought more generally. Is the current  age of pessimism and despair ending?
BURGIS: I think it might get worse  before it gets better. I hope it ends.
There’s been a lot of talk among friends of mine  who are very pro-tech accelerationists that the
pope is going to really come down on tech in  his new papal encyclical, which at the time of
our conversation is not out yet. There’s been  a lot of speculation about it. I think they’re
absolutely wrong, for instance, in that case.  I think he’s going to be very optimistic about
what AI can do for humanity, of course, with  some cautions about the way that it develops.
I think that even among my tech friends,  I’m seeing a lot of pessimism for
what a thinker like the pope might say  and not even giving him the benefit of
the doubt that we might be entering an age  where we can actually learn more about what
it means to be human than less. That might  lead to a renaissance in the humanities,
for instance. I think AI is performing a  kind of via negativa on the human person,
maybe even the human soul, in helping us  discover who we are. To me, that’s very exciting.
COWEN: I agree with you about the pope, but  if social contagion is such a dominant force,
how does the age of pessimism get turned around?  What’s the mechanism by which things will flip?
BURGIS: We need some more optimists, and then we  can hope for a good contagion with the optimists.
COWEN: Why doesn’t the negative  contagion just get stronger and
stronger and overwhelm everything, and  we all drown in a sea of terribleness?
BURGIS: The negative contagion and pessimism  can’t go on forever. I think that there are
cultural and societal release valves for  that kind of thing. Vibe shifts happen.
There’s the scapegoat mechanism. I don’t know  if we’ll talk about Girard today. I think that
there are things that correct. Sometimes  we over-correct. I just don’t see the
age of pessimism lasting. I think sometimes if  something happens that is traumatic and tragic,
like a serious war, even worse than the wars  that we currently see in the world today,
maybe it will take something like that to  actually help people build something. It
sounds a little bit paradoxical, but I think  sometimes optimism can arise out of tragedy.
COWEN: Why does it seem in the data, at least,  that the Anglo world is especially so unhappy?
BURGIS: The Anglo world, I think, especially  in the US, I really believe that we have some
bad ideas, what Byung-Chul Han has called  the achievement subject. It’s this very
Calvinist idea that I think has affected even  the way that we think about entrepreneurship,
which I’m extremely pro-entrepreneurship, but I  think that it’s in his book, The Burnout Society,
which was one of my favorite books. I  think he diagnoses the problem very well.
We’ve internalized this idea that we always  have to be doing something. There is always
more to achieve. We’ve forgotten some of  the fundamental things that actually make
for a good life. Family structures, people  are not having children. You and I have
talked about the fertility crisis before. I  think that that achievement subject mentality
has affected the West through everything  from media to our business culture.
I think we’re going to need to reevaluate that  as a society. I just got back from three and a
half weeks in Italy and I came back—I was going  to say I came back refreshed, but I traveled with
the toddler, so I can’t say that—I came back  wondering. For all of the economic stagnation
and problems that Italy has, do they also  have something right? People there actually
seem more joyful and optimistic, even than most  Americans that I know that are doing pretty well.
COWEN: As a critique of modernity, is  Dostoevsky or Thomas Mann more on the mark?
BURGIS: I’m very sympathetic to Thomas  Mann because I went to a seminary on
top of a hill in Italy for three years that  almost felt like a sanatorium in some ways.
I’m going to go with Dostoevsky, though,  because I think his book Demons diagnoses
what can happen at a psychic and spiritual level  when social contagion runs rampant. Of course,
having just written a book about social contagion,  I don’t think he’s mentioned in the book,
but Dostoevsky and some of the demonic elements,  whether you believe in demons or not, we can speak
of the demonic as something that seems to be  characterized by social contagion usually.
COWEN: Here’s a question from GPT, and I quote,
“Name the kind of person who reads  your book, takes the thesis sincerely,
applies it carefully, and yet ends up  worse off.” What’s the story there?
BURGIS: The new book or Wanting or both?
COWEN: The new book. Both,  but they’re of a piece, right?
BURGIS: They’re connected. Wanting is about  mimetic desire, and this book is a continuation
of that and how it plays out in social  dynamics, the self versus the crowd. I actually
think there’s a risk with my books and with any  nonfiction book or the exposure to any big idea,
especially one that purports to explain some  fundamental first principle about social life,
of thinking about it too much, making it a theory  of everything, over-psychologizing everything,
and losing sight of the concrete  realities and circumstances that we’re in.
To give you an example, it’s been  said that once a novelist reads the
work of René Girard and understands  mimetic theory and mimetic desire,
it will ruin them as a novelist because now they  don’t think that they have any original ideas,
everything’s just mimetic. The way out of that  problem actually is to stop thinking about it
so dang much and to not impose that frame on  everything and to get back to the concrete
and the particulars of life, which is a kind of  antidote. I’m not saying don’t reflect and don’t
think and that we shouldn’t think about these  things, but there is such a thing as overthinking.
COWEN: It’s a little bit like efficient  markets theory. Even if it’s true,
it’s better not to believe it?
BURGIS: Yes.
COWEN: Better for the world  and maybe better for you too.
Speaking of AI, will it make social contagion  stronger or weaker or in which ways?
BURGIS: I would bet that it’s going  to make social contagion weaker.
COWEN: Why?
BURGIS: Because we’re leaving the age of  information and entering what I would call the age
of intelligence. AI, to give one example, I think,  will lead to highly customized, personalized
education and learning experiences. People  being able to construct and follow. If you’re
an autodidact, I think it will be very good for  you because you’ll be able to follow ideas to the
end. We used to have to just read the footnotes  and try to track down obscure books. I think
AI will make that process a lot easier and more  exciting. That is not a mimetic process. It’s not
a social contagion process. That is using the AI  to follow your own intellectual interests. I could
probably think of other ways that it will make  us less contagious, but that’s just one of them.
COWEN: That might be part of what  flips us out of the pessimism?
BURGIS: I think so.
COWEN: Is that new emancipation?
BURGIS: I’m incredibly excited by that. I’m  thinking about my own writing and my own work.
I’ve got all kinds of blind spots and limitations.  When I write something or when I’m thinking about
something, asking the AI, what are all the  implications of what I’ve said here to a bunch
of domains of life that I don’t really know that  much about, I’m always amazed by what it says.
COWEN: What’s the story behind you  declining to work for Anthropic?
BURGIS: Well, it wasn’t to work for  them, just to set the record straight.
COWEN: Not to work for pay,  but to confer with them, right?
BURGIS: Just to confer with  them, yes. There’s a lot that I
don’t want to say, but I can tell you  more than I think I’ve said so far.
COWEN: Sure.
BURGIS: I always probe people’s motivations. In  this case, I had a back and forth with some folks
at Anthropic. I was asking basic questions like,  what’s next after this? They basically invited 14,
15 people out for a couple of days  to comment on Claude’s constitution.
I think they were all Christians, and  they were interested in virtue ethics and
what Christianity might have to add to  the development of making Claude be good.
I asked basic questions like, “What do you mean  by be? Philosophically, like that. What does that
mean? What does it mean for Claude to be good? It  seems like your discovery of virtue ethics, and
they were using the word discernment, is you’ve  landed on something that Ignatius and the Jesuits
had figured out 500 years ago. What’s next? Is  it just the two days, and what comes after that?”
The more that I talked to them—people do this all  the time; it’s why people like to meet the pope,
for instance—I didn’t know how genuine it was. I  thought that they were looking for a way to say,
“We did this thing, we conferred with  some Christians, we’re the good guys,
we’re building the good AI.” Then the way that it  was pitched to me was very much like, if I care
about the future and the good of humanity, then  this is definitely something that I could do.
It was framed like a moral imperative, not only  by people at Anthropic, but even by people that
know me, by fellow Christians. I said, “I  do think I have some moral responsibilities,
and there’s some moral imperatives in my  life, but flying out to San Francisco to
consult for Anthropic for free is not one  of them.” I don’t think that makes me a bad
person. It was just in the communication  with them, I felt like something was off.
COWEN: Just philosophically, putting  aside your theological views,
but what do you think of effective altruism  as a normative philosophy? That has guided,
at least, some parts of AI production, right?
BURGIS: Yes. It seems to have  guided many parts of it. I think
ultimately it hasn’t proved very successful in  doing some of the things that it set out to do.
I guess when we go back to the  beginning of effective altruism,
I’m unclear on how effectiveness is defined  by each person that practices it in different
ways. I don’t think that there’s enough  conversation on what the goals really are,
and it’s—and this will not surprise you—ultimately  very materialistic and doesn’t account for things
like the quality of relationships, depth,  culture. The things that can be measured,
usually with effective altruism, are often not the  things that I think are most important in life.
COWEN: If I ask you a question like,
why do men and women seem to be so far apart  these days, politically and aesthetically,
you think you would have a better answer  to that than the effective altruists would.
BURGIS: What’s their answer to that question?
COWEN: I’m not sure, but what’s your answer?
BURGIS: I’m not sure if that’s true.
COWEN: It’s political polarization. If you  poll them on politics, men are more right-wing.
BURGIS: Oh, we’re talking  specifically about politics.
COWEN: Women are more left-wing, but as you  know, measured sex seems to be going down;
certainly, childbearing,  which we measure pretty well,
is going down. Marriage is a more complicated  story, but for some socioeconomic groups,
it’s down. There’s just much less dating.  Everyone claims the dating apps are broken.
There was a piece in New Statesman about, in  Britain, angry young women are very upset at
the men that they encounter. It just seems to be  worse than usual, the gap between men and women?
BURGIS: Yes. I think technology is largely  to blame for that, the way that it sorts
things that it thinks men should see versus  things that women should see. It increases
the political polarization for everybody,  but in particular, between the genders,
I think that it plays a huge role. I think that  the way that men and women even meet each other,
the way that dating works, is very, very  different than the way that it used to be.
We often sort based on what we think our  preferences are before we’ve had a chance
to encounter a flesh and human person of the  opposite sex, and perceptions are formed,
often wrongly. The woman that I eventually  married, I never would have found her if I
was using a dating app, for instance.  I think technology has exacerbated
some of the false perceptions that we have  about the opposite sex and what people believe.
That’s especially true when it comes to  men and women because the algorithms,
the way that the social contagion  works, it knows that we are different.
We are men and women, and it exacerbates all of  the differences and doesn’t do much to promote
common understanding. I believe that men and women  are complementary, different but complementary,
and that’s not necessarily  a very popular view anymore.
COWEN: At what point does being  anti-mimetic itself become a mimetic
identity, and do you see some signs  of that in Silicon Valley? Everyone’s
supposed to be contrarian. There’s a  kind of false contrarianism. You don’t
even know anymore what’s a contrarian point of  view. Are we at that stage with Girardianism?
BURGIS: I think Girard would be  relatively mortified that mimetic
theory was very mimetic and so popular.  I think he himself worried about that,
and that was a running joke while he was still  alive in his circle at Stanford. I do think it’s
an issue. It goes back to why I said we shouldn’t  think about it too much. The book is titled The
One and the Ninety-Nine. The message, as  you know from having read it, is not that
everybody should become a rugged individualist  and that the goal is to become the one.
I think that’s incredibly dangerous. It’s  actually, in a world where all of the focus
is on the one, maybe we need to think more  actually about the 99 and the relationship
between the one and the 99 and the way that  the group and the self affect one another. I
think the focus has actually swung way too far  in the direction of the one. I mean, all of us
are the one in some sense, but the challenge of  today is how do we live in communities without
clustering in communities where everybody shares  the same values and thinks the same things?
Those are the most boring communities for me.  I don’t want to be in one of those communities,
but I get invited to them almost on  a daily basis, and I usually decline.
COWEN: Let’s say we put you in charge, either  of the government or of certain voluntary norms,
and you can change one thing. What’s the thing you
would change within the realm  of it being somewhat feasible?
BURGIS: In charge as a political leader or a CEO?
COWEN: You can either be dictator, or  you can be pope, or you can just be
the most influential person on moral  norms, and you can change one thing.
BURGIS: If I were the dictator of the United  States—my fiscally conservative friends
will hate this one—I think we lack mediating  intermediary institutions between individuals
in the state and that communities, places  are healthier to the extent that they have
these odd places in between, whether third  places or just intermediary institutions.
I would probably find a good musician in every  city who had some entrepreneurial spirit and was
interested in bringing people together—let’s  call it cities with over 100,000 people—and I
would give them startup funds to open jazz clubs  in every single city, and I would fund them from
my government. I would do probably a public  campaign to encourage—actually, I don’t know;
maybe the public campaign would backfire on  me because nobody likes being told what to do.
COWEN: Become too mimetic.
BURGIS: Forget that part. I think jazz  clubs in every city would go a long way
toward helping men and women. It would  probably actually go a long way toward
something nothing like jazz and alcohol to  help men and women learn to like each other.
COWEN: Changing a voluntary  social norm, what would you pick?
Like young men lose interest in pornography?
BURGIS: That one I’d definitely want to change.
COWEN: What’s at the top of your list?  It gives us a sense of your priorities.
BURGIS: It is. You named one that is at the top  of my list. I think it’s absolutely destroying
young men and women. The data is very clear  that women are watching a lot of porn, too. I
think that there are certain things that should be  made taboo. Porn is taboo in the sense that nobody
talks about it. I actually bring it up often  in my class because the data are something like
90 percent of the men in my class are watching  porn, and not quite that number with the women.
I’ll often bring it up in class, and then  I’m shocked at how many students over the
course of a few years actually come talk to me  about it. I’m actually relatively in favor of
introducing friction into the process and how  easy that stuff can be found. It’s being found
by accident. There was a story in the Free Press  last year. I think it was a 13-year-old girl found
it by accident. She said the discovery of it  has become like a rite of passage for people,
and it’s not even one that they’re seeking.  It just happens to them. I think there has
to be some friction introduced in  that process, and I would do that.
COWEN: In Girardian terms, is there  going to be a scapegoat that leads
to catharsis for us, or things remain unresolved?
BURGIS: My understanding of Girard is that that  world is gone, the world in which we can have a
scapegoat that will lead to catharsis.  We’re past that. We’ve seen too much.
One of his fundamental points is that  Christianity has created the conditions
for the runaway violence precisely  because the scapegoats don’t work anymore.
COWEN: Are we still in a  Christian society, ideologically?
BURGIS: Yes, absolutely. I think even people  that would consider themselves very secular
have obviously adopted a lot of Christian  ideas, in the West, I assume you mean.
COWEN: Sure, but say Japan. Is  Japan going to have a scapegoat?
BURGIS: It would be more likely for Japan to have  a scapegoat than for any country in the West. I
think we’re very much in a Christian society,  and there are some people on the integralist
right that don’t realize how Christian  of a society we actually do live in.
COWEN: You must know Rod Dreher. What do  you think of The Benedict Option? Withdraw.
BURGIS: I want to do Rod justice, and I  think it’s easy to strawman Rod and say
that he’s just recommending that everybody  move to a small farm. I don’t think that’s
what he’s saying. I think what he  gets right is that every person,
every family—my wife and I are thinking through  this right now—is going to have to probably,
in the world of social contagion, if it’s as bad  as some people think that it is, and I think that
there are many things that are bad, will have  to take certain actions to protect themselves.
If I don’t want my children watching porn  at a very young age, there’s certain things
that I’m going to have to do, and it will  involve putting boundaries between them
and the broader culture. I don’t think  it can be very prescriptive. I think
everybody’s case is very unique. I don’t plan  to move to Montana, but other people might.
COWEN: They have the internet in Montana. I  would worry all the more in Montana, right?
BURGIS: They have great internet in Montana.  I think that we live in a relatively Manichean
society. There’s a desire for purity. I  think the desire for purity is relatively
dangerous. It’s my disposition, I  think it’s my wife’s disposition,
to roll up my sleeves and just deal with  the messy world. I’ve noticed that every
time in my life where I’ve tried to flee it in  some way, I’ve actually ended up less happy.
COWEN: I’m not saying you’ll ever do it, but what  does your escape fantasy look like? One of mine is
I’ll go live in a third-tier city in Mexico. I’m  not going to do it, but sometimes I think about
it. Cost of living would be very low. The food  would be amazing. I could improve my Spanish.
BURGIS: It is moving to Genoa with my family,  making my US income, living in Italy. I love
Italy. I love the food. I love the people. I love  the culture. I feel lighter while I’m there. I
laugh more. We eat dinner later. I love everything  about it. It would probably be living in Italy for
the most part, or at least making that my home  base, brushing up on my Italian, working less.
COWEN: Why Genoa? It’s a wonderful city.  It’s still medieval, right, in a funny way?
BURGIS: It’s medieval. I think it’s  the most underrated city in Italy.
COWEN: In Italy, I mean, yes. I agree. Yes.
BURGIS: I think it’s the most  underrated city. You agree.
COWEN: I took my wife there. She was stunned. “How  come no one goes to Genoa?” She was telling me.
BURGIS: It’s close to Cinque Terre. It’s this city  that’s elevated. It has a fascinating history.
It was still a very functional port city. It  was really the most important city in Italy,
arguably the world, during when Spain was  a great power. It’s very cosmopolitan.
It reminds me of Marseille a little bit. It’s  vertical, breathtaking views. The people there,
they’re not very touristy. The Italians  there seem indifferent to you as a tourist.
It just feels very, very homey. It’s so  close to a lot of other great things in
Italy. You can get to Torino relatively  easily. That whole area up there, Bra,
where the Slow Food movement originated, you’re  just in striking distance from everything. Nobody
