I know that goes to Italy goes to Genoa. I plead  with them. I’m like, “Please, just go to Genoa.”
COWEN: I am the exception. My wife sometimes talks  of wanting to live in the smaller towns nearby,
which we’re not going to do because we’re  slated for a third-tier city in Mexico,
but we’re not going to do that either. I sometimes  think of Northern Italy as a place where there
were fewer different dimensions for mimetic  desire. That is, more people dress the same.
There are fewer status dimensions, maybe less  room for eccentrics compared to America. Do
you think that’s true, or do you think I’m off  base? Paris is a bit like this also. There’s a
certain notion of what kind of shoes an  Italian man should wear. They wear them,
and they’re amazing, and actually more affordable  than here. There’s a sameness to some things.
BURGIS: I don’t think the sameness is a bad  thing. I think the sameness is very charming.
The sprezzatura of an Italian man, the way that  an Italian man dresses, something I’ve never
been able to pull off in my life. For those  that don’t know what that sprezzatura means,
it means you put tremendous care into putting on  an outfit that looks like you didn’t think about
it at all, and somehow it comes together and looks  amazing. Even that seems highly mimetic to me,
the idea of sprezzatura. I love Naples. Naples  is maybe my second-favorite city in Italy.
COWEN: It’s my second favorite, too. Maybe  it’s my favorite. That and Genoa, to me,
are the two undiscovered, less discovered gems.
BURGIS: It makes sense why  we get along. Nobody goes to
Naples either. It’s too dirty. It’s  endless. I’ve heard all the excuses.
COWEN: It’s become somewhat more  popular, though. There’ve been some
New York Times articles. The food  has drawn some people, I think.
BURGIS: My test for whether or not I’ll get along  with somebody is their reactions to Naples after
they’ve been there. That’s my number one  test. To the Northern Italian question,
there’s a great book on Italy, if you haven’t  read it. It’s called The Italians by Luigi
Barzini in the ’60s. It’s just a fantastic book.  I think that the North has a little bit less of
the animated Italian gestures and spectacle  that you get in the South. It’s a little more
reserved. I would say that because of that,  it’s less mimetic than the South. I think that
disposition, that flamboyant way of being, is the  more mimetic thing about the South, about Naples.
COWEN: Speaking of Barzini, what do  you think of his hypothesis that the
face an Italian will show you,  in terms of level of cheeriness,
depends on how your status is perceived?  He thinks they’re somewhat of a sad people,
but they seem happy to outsiders because they  put on that face for the higher-status outsiders.
BURGIS: I wouldn’t disagree with Barzini  on Italian culture, so I’m not going to
disagree with him on that. He knows Italians much  better than I do. I think that the face in Italy,
maybe it’s like the smile in Thai. There’s  1,000 different smiles, and they all mean
something different. Italians are incredibly  good at reading the face and facial expressions,
but I think they have a different standard for  foreigners like me than they do for each other.
COWEN: How is Italian Catholicism different?
BURGIS: Depends on what part of Italy you’re in.
COWEN: Say, Genoa, whatever part you know best.
BURGIS: I think that, having spent a few weeks  there very recently and went to mass quite a
few times—I was there during Holy Week—it is  aesthetically very different. You typically
will walk into a very old church that has no  heating or AC, has absolutely terrible acoustics,
and you’ll find people wandering in and  out, like you would in an orthodox church.
It’s like walking around. I would say that it’s  relatively low liturgy compared to what you see.
A lot of the revival in Catholicism here in  the US are high-liturgy things. I actually
found it to be somewhat difficult. I couldn’t  even hear the priests most of the time because
the sound system is really bad. I think that  the liturgy is really the test for me about
everything else that’s going on, and that’s the  sacramental life. The first thing I notice about
any Catholic church is how many times they  offer confession. I look at it right away,
and I can tell you 10 other things about that same  church and predict it with a very high degree.
COWEN: What does that tell  you? Let’s say they offer
confession frequently. What do you then infer?
BURGIS: I infer that it’s thriving. One could say  they offer confession frequently because they just
have a lot of people there that believe in the  sacrament of confession. I think it’s quite the
opposite. It turns out from every priest that  I’ve talked to that if you offer confession
frequently, maybe a few times a week or  daily, the lines just start to form. It’s
actually quite the opposite. You’ll have a lot  of priests that just start offering it more.
The extremes are confessions available by  appointment only on Saturdays versus confession
before every mass. That is the number one signal  for me, and then how often they have adoration.
This is Catholic inside baseball here. It is like  politics. If I know your position on gun control,
I can, with a high degree of accuracy, predict  your position on 10 other clustered things.
COWEN: Why is it that, at least in formal terms,  Italy has become so nonreligious? I get that
underneath the cultural structure, it may be quite  Catholic still, but the number of people who go
to church or who profess, say, a belief in the  Trinity seems fairly low. How did that happen?
BURGIS: It seems like they’re almost tired of  their Catholicism. They’ve had it for so long.
It almost seems like cultural Judaism  to me. It’s maybe like the familiarity
breeds contempt. I don’t know, but that’s the  sense that I get. Like some politics in Italy,
I think Mussolini had something to do with it,  the Christian Democrats. I think that it was
such a part of their identity for so long, it  wasn’t handed down by the last few generations,
and there’s just a sense in  which it has become cultural.
I met many Italians on this last trip  that would make the sign of the cross
if they heard an ambulance drive by or they  walked by an image of Madonna on a street
corner or something like that, but they  probably haven’t been to mass in years.
This has become very cultural. I don’t  know why, but I think that they’re tired.
COWEN: What was it like  living next to Vatican City?
BURGIS: Speaking of this, I was mortified when  one day I had to walk directly by St. Peter’s
very often just to get home up on the Janiculum  Hill. I walked by St. Peter’s one day and I didn’t
look at it, I didn’t think about it, and then I  was mortified and I realized it was too late to
go back because I had to be somewhere. Rome can  be a very difficult place to live as a person of
faith. When I got there, somebody said, Rome  will either strengthen your faith or lose it
as a Catholic because you will see  the dark underbelly of everything.
You will see a lot of worldliness and you will  either come out of it with a more supernatural
vision of what the church is or you will come  out of it with your tail between your legs,
really worried about things. For me, it was really  not one of those two extremes. It was like I came
out of it not that much different than when I  went in. It was probably the three most formative
years of my life when I lived next to the Vatican  because it was an incredibly strange situation.
I was a 31-year-old man who had owned  my own house in Las Vegas and suddenly
lived in what was essentially a dormitory with  250 other men, most of them younger than me.
The typical age for a seminarian is 20,  25 probably, with a shared bathroom on
every floor. Talk about a relatively mimetic  environment where we share so much in common.
I would also say because of that, it was one of  the funniest places that I’ve ever been because
one of the ways that you learn to live in  a situation like that is through comedy.
COWEN: Why didn’t you become a priest?
BURGIS: John Henry Newman said that  one should never tell the story of
their conversion or their vocational  discernment between tea and dessert.
It’s just too complex of a question. The easy  answer that I’ll give you, it’s not a cop-out,
is that I carefully discerned for a number  of years that it was not what I felt like I
was being called to do. I’ll tell you one of the  little parts of that story that helped me realize
that. I was studying theology at a pontifical  university in Rome, right in Piazza Navona.
I was on my way to a fundamental theology  class in my second year in Rome. I was having
nagging doubts. Something felt a little bit  off in my discernment process. It turned out
that there was a Matthew Luhn who was a Pixar  animator. He played an instrumental role in
the development of the first Toy Story. He  was a storyboard guy. He worked with all of
these guys at Pixar. He happened to be in Rome  giving a master class on storytelling that day.
This is a very typical Italian story. The venue  you’re supposed to give the workshop at in Rome
did not allow him in due to some kind of  bureaucratic maintenance of the building.
COWEN: Very Italian already.
BURGIS: It’s incredibly Italian. He had to find an  emergency place to hold his workshop, and he held
it at my pontifical university. I don’t know the  backstory there, but he was there. I saw a sign,
“Matthew Luhn, Pixar, storytelling master class.”  It was not cheap. All these Italians paid to go.
I talked my way in, and I skipped class, and I  went to the storytelling class that day. I was so
lit up by that class that I realized that there  was something in me that craved this creative,
artistic, aesthetic thing. I think it ruined  theology for me for the rest of the year.
COWEN: Aesthetics trumped theology?
BURGIS: Von Balthasar wrote a whole aesthetic  treatise, the theological aesthetics. Theology
and aesthetics go hand in hand, really. He  understood the whole story of the incarnation,
like the acts of a play. I think that I’m  very much a von Balthasar Catholic in the
sense that I do see a lot of the goodness and  beauty and aesthetic characteristics of the
church as related to truth. It’s one of the ways  that we can come to the truth is through beauty.
COWEN: Aesthetically, what is  it in Christianity that’s most
important to you personally? If  it were me—I’m not Christian—but
I might say Bach’s B minor mass or maybe  Monteverdi’s Vespers. What would you say?
BURGIS:
Aesthetically, it is the liturgy. It is  a beautifully celebrated Catholic mass.
I’m not one of these pre-Vatican II guys  where I think that the Latin mass is the
only real mass. I do think that is incredibly  beautiful, though. I go to it every once in a
while because I think it’s very beautiful. I  actually came back to my faith through that
practice. It’s not one particular thing or piece  of artwork for me; it is the beauty of the ritual.
We’ve lost ritual in the world today in many  cases. Seeing that, seeing the reverence,
seeing a church full of people shoulder  to shoulder on their knees in itself is
beautiful to me. I remember just seeing  everybody drop to their knees for the
first time when I went back to mass after not  having gone in a very long time. I remember
being struck by that’s not something I  would see anywhere else in the world.
COWEN: If I speak to people who are Ethiopian  Christians or maybe Egyptian Coptic Christians,
possibly Armenian Christians, they will  communicate a sense that somehow they’re
in tune with an earlier, more fundamental  Christianity than what we have in many other
places. Does that argument carry any weight  with you? Are you tempted by that or no?
BURGIS: A little bit. I don’t think that  it’s true, but I’m very attracted to

alterity, that I think the Eastern  Orthodox liturgy preserves in a way

COWEN: Do we need Protestantism in America  to keep print culture front and center?

BURGIS: I love my Protestant brothers and sisters,  so I don’t want them to go away. I might want them

I think generally good things do come out of  tension, and yes, the church is oral to more

COWEN: Sure. UAPs, yes.
BURGIS: —but it seems as if even  this discourse that we’re in right

BURGIS: I don’t find it crazy either,  as one who believes in demons. That’s

BURGIS: Well, demons are fundamental to  Christianity. The gospels are full of

BURGIS: Well, given what you’ve just shared,  I probably would be if I learned more about

BURGIS: Well, I never started a business in Italy.

BURGIS: I ended up walking away from a company  in my late 20s to take up some time off,

BURGIS: It’s just wonderful.

BURGIS: Yes. I try not to talk about  Michigan too much because Northern

COWEN: Now, your own Cluny Institute, do  you think of it as closer to a monastery,
a salon, a talent network, a way of  organizing a Christian counter elite,
all of those? How’s the way you would  present what it is or what it does?
BURGIS: I would think of it as trying  to build a talent network and forming a
kind of artist colony and workshop for people  that have a religious sense or sensibility,
that are open to the transcendent, that  are smart, that care about serious ideas,
and that want to build real things in the world,  that really care about the vector of innovation.
It’s not just building, but it’s like a step  back, what should we be building? Trying to
find as many of those people as possible in the  world. It’s got a couple of different functions.
One of them is it’s trying to operate as a bat  signal, putting things out into the world that
bring the right people out of the woodwork. That’s  certainly happening. Then there’s a part of it
where I want to work with people that are able to  work at the intersection of what I call Athens,
Jerusalem, and Silicon Valley. We don’t have to  silo those things. I think that Silicon Valley,
for instance, would be healthier if it actually  wasn’t as allergic to religious thinking,
for instance. I think religious thinking  could do Silicon Valley a lot of good. I’m
betting that if we can begin to find that  network, and invest in that talent network,
that 10 or 20 years from now, it will be  building some of the most important things in
the world. I don’t just mean companies. I mean  cultural things, aesthetic things, workshops,
things that will produce new forms of community,  maybe even a model for a new institution.
The reason that I am so struck by the story of  the original Cluny is that it was an entirely
new kind of institution in its day. Even legally  speaking, right? Its original charter, the guy
that gave all of the money renounced his right to  have anything to do with the way that it operated.
It formed a network of over 1,200 Cluniac  monasteries. My imagination is struck by,
“Well, what does that look like today if  we can have networked workshops of people
that are all drawing inspiration, and talking  about ideas that are open to the religious sense?”
COWEN: The original Cluny was also a pioneer  of accounting techniques. Is that correct?
BURGIS: I know that a Franciscan invented  double-entry accounting. I know that,
but he wasn’t associated with Cluny.  There were all kinds of innovations,
architectural innovations, agricultural,  winemaking innovations that happened. It
was really the largest church in the world for 300  years, the most important institution in Europe,
in my opinion. It was the center of innovation  in Europe, out of the liturgical renewal that
it instituted, and it welcomed people in.  Monasteries, the Benedictine tradition,
has always been known for hospitality. No matter  who you were, if you’re sick, if you’re poor,
if you’re traveling, if you’re a pilgrim, you  could knock on the door, and you would be let in,
and you could stay for a day or two or longer,  and then you would be sent on your way.
Cluny actually popularized the Camino de Santiago.  They’re the first ones that would send people on
the Camino de Santiago. I could go on and on about  all the things that Cluny did, but the people that
came into contact with it—it was worldly in  the sense that it interacted with politicians,
with builders, with the Romanesque, the masons in  Italy. It was incredibly worldly in that it opened
its door to all of those people and interacted  with them, and then somehow shaped them. Is
there a lay version of that? I’m obviously not  trying to build a monastery. I’m not a monk,
but I’m inspired by the way that it existed in the  world as a sign of something completely different.

BURGIS: I hope I can deal with it  as good as he has dealt with his.

BURGIS: I plan to be building  Cluny for a very long time.

BURGIS: Probably in Italy.

BURGIS: Thanks for having me, Tyler.
